query: What sample sizes or power calculations do we need for the planned logistic, Cox, and Poisson models given plausible effect sizes and baseline rates?

response.query: What sample sizes or power calculations do we need for the planned logistic, Cox, and Poisson models given plausible effect sizes and baseline rates?
response.answer: For logistic, Cox, and Poisson models, sample size depends on effect size, baseline rate, and desired power (typically 80%); use power analysis tools like G*Power or statistical software to calculate. Generally, larger sample sizes are needed for rare events.

results.content: St. John’s Medical College and Research Institute, Bangalore, (Division of Clinical Research and Training, DCRT) has been conducting short-term courses on health research methods since 2009. St. John’s Medical College and Research Institute, Bangalore, (Division of Clinical Research and Training, DCRT) has been conducting short-term courses on health research methods since 2009. The topics for the course included research hypotheses, cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, cohort studies, randomized controlled trials, diagnostic research, evaluating treatments, systematic review, meta-analysis, health policy and advocacy, qualitative studies, research ethics, grants writing, scientific publications, data management, basics of Epi-Info/ SPSS and biostatistics (types of variables, sampling methods, sample size calculation, descriptive statistics, inferential statistics - t tests, chi squared tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, univariate, multi-variate regression and survival analysis).

results.title: Occupational Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica
results.content: OSHA believes that if the most recent cost estimates had been used, they would have had a minor effect on Inforum's estimate of the employment impact of the final rule. OSHA used the exposure-response models from these studies in a life table analysis to estimate excess risk of disease mortality from exposure to respirable crystalline silica after accounting for competing causes of death due to background causes. Section 6(b)(5) of the OSH Act states: “The Secretary, in promulgating standards dealing with toxic materials or harmful physical agents under this subsection, shall set the standard which most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, on the basis of the best available evidence, that no employee will suffer material impairment of health or functional capacity even if such employee has regular exposure to the hazard dealt with by such standard for the period of his working life.” Given that OSHA must analyze significant risk over a working life, the Agency estimated benefits for the affected population over the same period.

results.content: Phil Rosen Award for the Best Abstract on Clinical or Epidemiology Research by a Trainee 7 Effectiveness of the Making it Work™ Program at Improving Presenteeism and Work Cessation in Workers with Inflammatory Arthritis – Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial Andre Luquini (University of British Columbia - Department of Experimental Medicine / Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Yufei Zheng (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Hui Xie (Arthritis Research Canada/Faculty of Health Sciences at Simon Fraser University, Richmond); Catherine Backman (Rehab Sciences/Occupational Therapy, University of British Columbia, Richmond); Pamela Rogers (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Alex Kwok (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Astrid Knight (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Monique Gignac (Institute for Work and Health, Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto, Toronto); Dianne Mosher (University of Calgary, Calgary); Linda Li (Rehab Sciences/Physical Therapy, University of British Columbia, Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); John Esdaile (University of British Columbia (Division of Rheumatology)/Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Carter Thorne (University of Toronto (Division of Rheumatology) / Southlake Regional Health Centre, Newmarket); Diane Lacaille (University of British Columbia (Division of Rheumatology)/ Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond) Objectives: Arthritis often leads to presenteeism (decreased at-work productivity) and permanent work disability, the worst occupational outcome of a disease, leading to reduced quality of life and cost to society.
